summary:
**Abandoned but Not Forgotten** is an interactive educational experience that brings the stories of NASA’s space explorers and their journeys to life. We developed a browser-based application featuring an interactive solar system, 19 spacecraft and exploration entries, character-led storytelling, planetary information, six interactive Science Lab tools, and a mission quiz with progress tracking.

The project addresses the challenge by helping users discover what happened to spacecraft and equipment after their missions ended—whether they remain on the Moon or other planetary surfaces, continue orbiting, have gone silent, or have completed their missions. Through engaging narratives and interactive exploration, the application turns mission history and scientific information into an accessible learning experience.

Our goal is to show that space exploration does not end when a mission is over. The equipment left behind represents years of human curiosity, engineering, discovery, and scientific achievement. By sharing these stories, we hope to make planetary exploration more engaging and ensure these remarkable explorers are not forgotten.
details:
Project Details – Abandoned but Not Forgotten

What does the project do and how does it work?

Abandoned but Not Forgotten is an interactive, browser-based space exploration experience that helps users discover the stories of spacecraft and exploration equipment across our Solar System. Users begin with an interactive 3D solar system, select planets or other destinations, and explore the missions and spacecraft associated with them. The application features 19 explorer entries, individual mission stories, scientific facts, and an Explorer Family archive that tracks discoveries and saves progress on the user's device.

It also includes six interactive Science Lab tools: Planet Comparison, Age on Other Planets, Weight on Other Planets, Day and Night, Orbits, and Moon Counts. A mission quiz reinforces learning, while character-led conversations make complex mission histories easier to understand.

What benefits does it have?

The project makes space science more engaging and accessible by combining scientific information with exploration, storytelling, and interactive learning. Instead of simply reading mission descriptions, users can navigate the Solar System, discover spacecraft, compare planetary characteristics, test their knowledge, and track their progress. It encourages curiosity and helps learners understand the scientific contributions of missions even after their operational lives have ended.

What is the intended impact?

Our intended impact is to preserve the stories of humanity's space exploration efforts and inspire interest in planetary science, astronomy, engineering, and future missions. We want users to recognise that spacecraft and equipment left behind are not meaningless debris; they represent important scientific achievements, engineering milestones, and valuable historical records. The project also encourages awareness of the different outcomes of space missions, including active, silent, retired, and completed explorers.

What tools and technologies were used?

The project was developed as a single-page web application using:

  • HTML5 – application structure and content.
  • CSS3 – responsive layouts, visual design, animations, and transitions.
  • JavaScript – interactive features, mission data, navigation, quizzes, and progress tracking.
  • Three.js – interactive 3D planetary and solar-system visualisations.
  • HTML Canvas and SVG – custom space backgrounds, visual effects, and interface graphics.
  • Web Audio API – synthesised interface sounds and audio effects.
  • Local Storage – saving user preferences and exploration progress on the device.
  • Google Fonts – Inter, Space Grotesk, and IBM Plex Mono for typography.

No specialised physical hardware was required; the application runs in a modern web browser.

How is the project creative?

The project's central creative approach is to turn spacecraft into characters with stories to tell. Users explore as a new probe, guided through the experience by a character named Navgrah. Fictional conversations inspired by real mission histories create an emotional connection with the explorers, while clearly distinguishing these conversations from actual NASA transmissions. The combination of a 3D Solar System, cinematic transitions, interactive dashboards, progress tracking, and storytelling creates an experience that blends education with exploration.

What factors did the team consider?

We considered scientific accuracy, ease of navigation, educational value, accessibility, responsiveness across screen sizes, and user engagement. We included different mission-status categories to help users understand whether an explorer is still active, has gone silent, has been retired, or has completed its mission. We also considered reduced-motion preferences, touch-based interaction, readable information panels, and locally saved progress. Planetary visuals are presented as illustrative rather than to scale, and fictional storytelling is identified as a creative interpretation of real mission history.
